We present AnnalsChallenge: 50 formalised theorem statements written by hand in Lean 4 using Mathlib. Each is the main result of a paper published in the Annals of Mathematics since 2020. Every formalisation was manually reviewed and then audited by AI. We release them without formalised proofs.

title: Masked Diffusion for Travel Diaries Synthesis
summary: Because household travel surveys combine household characteristics, variable-length person rosters, vehicle rosters, and trip chains, existing synthesis pipelines split them across separate models or flatten them into cropped fixed-length vectors. Representation, rather than modeling, becomes the bottleneck: splitting severs cross-segment dependence, and cropping truncates the household-structure distribution. We instead tokenize the diary and keep the object whole: each household-day becomes one token sequence with count tokens for vehicles, persons, and trips, and distinct symbols for padded, hidden, unobserved, and inapplicable positions. We introduce DiaryBridge, a masked diffusion model that bridges the fully hidden sequence to the distribution of complete diaries by unmasking positions in any order. One trained model, conditioned on any observed subset, performs synthesis and partial-diary completion alike. Experiments on real data extracted from the 2017/2018 Regional Travel Survey of the Baltimore region show that DiaryBridge generates travel reflecting vehicle availability and employment status, recovers shared trips using other household members' observed diaries, and better reproduces aggregate demand across modes, purposes, and departure periods than the learned baselines.

title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
summary: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

title: Efficient Safety Guardrails through Latent Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning with On-Demand Trace Reconstruction
summary: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.

title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
summary: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

title: Hallucination-aware Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

title: Complex materials engineering via Provenance Action Graphs: potential, structure and demonstration
summary: This work discusses and tests the potential of reaction graphs for material synthesis, in which events consist of reaction steps (actions) and their outputs (observations). The importance comes from the requirement to synthesize technologically useful materials, especially those that are kinetically stabilized. Often, it is a science that follows years of trial and error, culminating in (published) successful recipes, but is truly driven by far more (unpublished) failures. The entry into the era of AI provides an opportunity to use learning algorithms to encode rules from multi-dimensional synthesis pathways, regardless of their technological usefulness, and to decode both forward prediction and inverse learning modes. The main incentive is to accelerate material discovery by generating a global knowledge base that can be shared among data agents and contributed to by them. We will focus on several scenarios in the common synthesis process during solid-state synthesis, primarily because these reactions are kinetic in nature and require closer monitoring and control of the reaction history.

title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
summary: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. This expectation holds only if padded rows are removed from both the numerator and the softmax normalizer. Common implementation idioms meet it only under side conditions. Zeroing padded features alone does not work. Masking logits with $-\infty$ fails on empty bags and on nonfinite padding. Masking with a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. We define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any finite number of masked rows with arbitrary real features and logits. We also prove that values at masked positions are irrelevant and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. The theorems hold for arbitrary finite index types and feature dimensions. Using the jax-lean certificate pipeline, we connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the JAX kernel itself. Lean checks translation certificates for two concrete shapes, identifies the generated functions with the generic specification, and transfers both invariances to the imported Jaxpr's real-arithmetic semantics. All audited theorems depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. The results concern ideal real arithmetic. Floating-point execution, XLA, and the JAX tracer and importer remain outside the proof.

title: SchemaPose: RGB-Based Category-Level Pose Estimation with Parametric Category Schema
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://souglad21.github.io/SchemaPose/
summary: RGB-based category-level 9D pose estimation remains highly challenging because a monocular system must generalize across unseen object instances while jointly inferring 3D translation, 3D rotation, and 3D size. Unlike instance-level pose estimation, the category-level setting requires the network to learn both what is shared across objects within a category and how individual instances vary in structure. This challenge is amplified in the RGB-only setting, where pose cues, category-level commonality, and instance-specific variation are entangled in appearance without direct geometric constraints, making it difficult for existing frameworks to learn a representation that is truly aligned with the category-level estimation objective. To address this problem, we propose SchemaPose, a schema-guided framework for RGB-based category-level pose estimation. SchemaPose equips the estimation pipeline with an explicit parametric schema for modeling category-level regularities together with structured instance variation, and uses the inferred schema variables to guide pose-related prediction in an end-to-end query-based framework. The same formulation also supports template instantiation, synthetic annotation, and pose learning within a unified framework. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that SchemaPose achieves state-of-the-art performance among RGB-based methods for category-level 9D pose estimation.

title: AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents
summary: Training business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce AssetForge, an asset-augmented task-construction pipeline that pairs a reusable construction-asset library with task-specific Rubrics. The assets provide application interfaces, world-state components, policy/evidence carriers, and native assertion definitions; the Rubric directs their instantiation for a particular business task. Executable checks and an additional model-based review validate each candidate, return targeted feedback, and support bounded repair before acceptance. On AutomationBench v1.0.6 public-600, fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 6,000 AssetForge examples yields 41.17% on the official strict pass@1 metric, 4.4 times the 9.33% base score (+31.83 points). With the same backbone and GLM-5.3 supervision, AssetForge reaches 41.17% versus 30.33% for traditional Rubrics, a 10.84-point gain (35.7% relative) at the same accepted-example scale (6,000 versus 6,000 examples). Both DeepSeek- and GLM-supervised AssetForge models improve AppWorld completion over the base model on Test-Normal and Test-Challenge. These results establish the advantage of AssetForge's complete construction pipeline on AutomationBench public: the coupled asset-Rubric interface directs Authors toward business logic, while executable checks and model-based review validate their tasks.

title: OpenDGO: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Organizations Across Diverse Application Domains
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems are increasingly applied across diverse domains, yet different applications require different forms of agent organization. Existing studies typically adopt predefined organizations, such as Star, Chain, and Tree, or learn communication graphs to improve performance on specific tasks. However, these methods are largely designed and evaluated within a limited set of application domains, providing little understanding of whether an organization effective in one domain remains suitable for others with different collaboration requirements. We present \textbf{OpenDGO}, a controlled benchmark and analysis framework covering six real-world domains and three collaboration settings: Sequential Dependency, Parallel Decomposition, and Information Integration. Under matched tasks, agents, tools, and resource limits, OpenDGO compares fixed and learned organizations while separately examining communication graphs, role assignments, input assignments, resource budgets, and component failures. Our results show that there is no ``one-organization-for-all'' solution: preferred organizations vary across applications, and even the same communication graph can yield different outcomes under different role and input assignments. These findings highlight the need for application-dependent organization design, aiming to understand \emph{which organization is suitable for a given application, under what conditions, and why}.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching
summary: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
comment: NeurIPS workshop on Foundations of Agentic Systems Theory (FAST), 2026
summary: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs $N$ compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.

title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
summary: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM

title: ReDiS: Reasoning-Diagnosis Self-Evolution for Multimodal Reasoning in Remote Sensing
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.

title: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution
summary: We introduce \textbf{ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER)}, a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. Within a single unified model, ABot-ER commands specialist-level depth across all three competencies, spanning spatial, scene, and temporal reasoning in perception; long-horizon action organization in planning; and point grounding and affordance in execution. The \textbf{Agentic Data-Model Self-Evolution Engine} continuously adapts data strategies to the model's evolving capability state. The \textbf{Task-Conditioned Adaptive Training Strategy} uses task tokens to activate lightweight low-rank residuals over a shared backbone, separating updates from heterogeneous output formats while retaining shared embodied knowledge. Across a systematic evaluation on twelve benchmarks covering three core competencies and five capability dimensions, ABot-ER achieves \textbf{state-of-the-art overall performance} across perception, planning, and execution within a unified parametric framework, demonstrating that breadth and depth can coexist in unified embodied reasoning.

title: ModRes: A modification of the ResPlan dataset ready for floor plan analysis and graph machine learning
summary: Floor plan datasets underpin computational analysis of building layouts, spatial connectivity and graph machine learning. However, publicly available datasets often require substantial preprocessing before they can be used reliably. We present ModRes, a cleaned and enriched version of the ResPlan dataset, containing 8,431 valid and unique residential floor plans. Invalid and duplicate floor plans are removed through a dedicated cleaning workflow, producing a ready-to-use dataset. For each floor plan, ModRes provides two-dimensional geometry, images, three-dimensional building representations and three complementary dual graphs in CSV and JSON formats with graph-, node- and edge-level features. Continuous and categorical graph attributes support machine learning workflows. We characterise the dataset using graph-based statistics and demonstrate its utility through a range of case studies. ModRes provides structured geometric, topological and semantic representations needed to automate spatial analysis and support machine learning-based workflows for building design and performance evaluation.

title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal

title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
summary: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. Constrained by a knowledge infrastructure (KI) and a validation convention, agents define parameter domains, observation mappings and objectives, and generate model-specific code. GCH checks the formulations against the same declarations and freezes them before numerical search and assessment, which require no further agent judgement. Agent-authored workflows executed across six model families, with assessment identifying unmet criteria. In snow-model tests, five of five knowledge-guided specifications executed on the first attempt, compared with none of five given only the model name, achieving validation Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.81-0.94 against 0.57 for defaults. Under a common objective, independent GR4J formulations yielded scores within 0.001 NSE; re-evaluating eleven saved parameter vectors reproduced their metrics. In ten paired VIC tests with matched budgets, fixed search was non-inferior to continuing agent proposals (margin, -0.02 NSE; median difference, -0.003). This separation enables end-to-end calibration delegation with inspectable scientific choices and reproducible numerical evaluation.

title: CartoVec: General-Purpose Location Embeddings from Open Map Data
summary: Geographic coordinates are common inputs in applied machine learning, but latitude and longitude describe position rather than the surrounding environment. Image-grounded location encoders learn this context from satellite or ground-level imagery; structured open map data offers another source of supervision whose utility for continuous coordinate encoders remains less explored. We introduce CartoVec, a coordinate encoder trained to predict Overture-derived land cover, land use, transportation, place and connectivity targets at multiple spatial scales, without image inputs or downstream-task labels. We evaluate frozen embeddings on Census outcomes, Airbnb prices and Philadelphia crime in the US Northeast using spatial block cross-validation. CartoVec has the highest mean performance on most Census outcomes and the highest average across the full suite, with several comparisons close across folds. The findings support open map data as a practical source of reusable location representations with a coordinate-to-vector interface that requires no map lookup at inference. The open-weight model is available at https://huggingface.co/gursoyfurkan/CartoVec.

title: Resource-Efficient 3D Shape and Orientation Estimation of Road Users using Roadside RGB Camera and 3D Radar
comment: Accepted at the 18th IEEE Symposium Sensor Data Fusion: Trends, Solutions and Applications (SDF 2026), Bonn, Germany
summary: End-to-end deep learning pipelines for camera-radar 3D object detection are well established in driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles; however, adapting them to roadside-mounted infrastructure presents significant challenges. On vehicles, sensor heights, pitch angles, and relative geometries remain largely uniform, allowing end-to-end models to generalize effectively. On the contrary, roadside sensor installations vary drastically in height, tilt, and field of view across locations, rendering end-to-end models prone to failure and difficult to adapt without massive location-specific datasets. Hence, instead of designing a complex end-to-end pipeline for direct 3D bounding box estimation, a low-cost, resource-efficient two-stage approach is proposed for real-time 3D shape and orientation estimation. The first stage utilizes any off-the-shelf, state-of-the-art method to extract 2D camera bounding boxes and associated 3D radar points for each road user. The proposed second stage then processes these inputs to construct 3D oriented bounding boxes where radar data determines 3D position, predefined templates define size for each road user, and a tiny neural network predicts a site-specific and optimized yaw angle. The algorithm is successfully validated at a curved road with a junction for pedestrians, bicycles, and cars, where it achieves 25 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson ORIN for real-time applications.

title: The Singularity Has a Distribution: Exact Timing Laws and Detection Limits for a Stochastic Intelligence Explosion
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/xiaoyulics/singularity-distribution
summary: Automating AI research creates a positive feedback loop between software capability and research effort. We study a stochastic realisation of this loop in which independent, positive, multiplicative improvements arrive at a rate proportional to a power of current capability. Within this model, randomness leaves the deterministic explosion threshold unchanged but replaces the blow-up date by an explicit distribution. For equal-sized improvements the explosion time is a geometrically weighted sum of independent exponentials; its $q$-series representation gives its transforms, moments and tail behaviour, including a two-term small-time asymptotic. For Lomax-distributed improvement sizes the explosion time is exactly Gamma distributed. Self-similarity implies that, with parameters known, the relative uncertainty about the remaining time does not vanish as explosion approaches. We formulate a fixed-sample test between constant and geometrically increasing idea-arrival rates. If the baseline rate and the alternative log-rate increment $\ell$ are known, the minimum sample size at error level $α$ is asymptotic to $(12z_α^2)^{1/3}\ell^{-2/3}$, where $z_α$ is the upper-$α$ standard normal quantile. Uncertainty about the growth exponent near its critical value produces a $1/t$ tail with an explicit constant, and hence an infinite conditional mean waiting time, although explosion is certain given a positive exponent. Separate extensions show that a fixed deployment delay prevents explosion in the specified delayed-feedback models, that power-law diversion of effort shifts the growth threshold, and that in a deterministic oversight race a fixed allocation share does not change the asymptotic regime, except at a critical equality of exponents. Numerical illustrations, which are not empirical forecasts, show how timing and detectability depend on the granularity of improvements.

title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
summary: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.

title: CoTL: Compact Token Learning for 3D Scene Representation
summary: We present CoTL, a framework that learns a compact set of tokens that preserves scene geometry and appearance from unposed multi-view images. Our encoder compresses the input images into small per-view sets of latent tokens that aggregate information across views to form a view-consistent scene representation. Each additional view expands the representation with only a small, resolution-independent set of tokens, allowing its capacity to grow with the available observations. To force this compact bottleneck to retain sufficient scene information, a query-based Gaussian decoder uses scene-independent queries to attend to the learned tokens and recover an explicit, renderable set of 3D Gaussian primitives. Novel-view rendering supervision trains the compact representation end to end through the reconstructed Gaussian scene. Experiments on \retenk{} and ACID show that the resulting compact, unstructured token set supports competitive novel-view synthesis and can serve as the latent space of a generative model for 3D Gaussian scene generation. Together, these results show that 3D Gaussian reconstruction is an effective objective for compact scene representation learning and the learned token space provides a basis for broader downstream tasks in 3D vision.

title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
summary: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.

title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.

title: EmoGenie: Benchmarking and Evaluating Expressed and Evoked Emotion in T2I Generation with MLLMs
comment: Comments: Corresponding author: Xiongkuo Min. Equal contribution: Zixuan Xing and Lancheng Gao
summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
summary: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
comment: 45 pages, 5 figures. Website: https://rogy-labs.github.io/tutorduel/ Code: https://github.com/RoGy-Labs/tutorduel-code Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/romainpuech/tutorduel
summary: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

title: $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP: Plug-and-Play Denoising for Scientific Imaging with Self-Supervised Score Priors
summary: Modern image restoration methods increasingly rely on large-scale supervised training, yet clean targets are often prohibitively difficult to obtain in scientific imaging modalities such as hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Plug-and-play ADMM (PnP-ADMM) with pretrained diffusion priors offers a promising alternative, but the learned prior distribution can mismatch both the target scientific image distribution and the distribution of ADMM denoiser inputs induced by dual feedback. To mitigate these mismatches, we propose $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP, a self-supervised plug-and-play restoration framework that learns a score prior directly from observation-derived ADMM intermediate states, without clean training targets or externally pretrained weights. Specifically, the learned score corrects the input to the analytical prior update, combining observation-driven corrections with analytical regularization. We further analyze the convergence and reconstruction error of the corrected ADMM algorithm assuming an ideal score and quadratic data fidelity. Experiments on reference-guided HSI restoration, single-image HSI denoising, and MRI denoising demonstrate consistent improvements over competing methods.

title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
summary: Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long-running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm-10K, a high-quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self-recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self-improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, our ReTerm-9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
summary: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.

title: MFVSR: A Multi-Style and Fine-Grained Benchmark for Video Subtitle Removal
comment: 31 pages, including appendix. Code: https://github.com/hxyiiii/MFVSR ; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/siiian/MFVSR
summary: Video subtitle removal (VSR) is an important video restoration task, yet existing evaluation remains limited by low-resolution datasets, fragmented test sets, and generic video-inpainting protocols that fail to adequately capture localized restoration errors, unintended modifications, temporal instability, and incomplete outputs. In this paper, we introduce MFVSR, a large-scale multi-style benchmark for fine-grained and reliability-aware video subtitle removal evaluation. MFVSR distinguishes itself through three key features: (1) Large-scale and diverse data, comprising 3,000 paired videos from Real-HQ, Real-LQ, and AI-Generated sources, with an auxiliary set of 953 in-the-wild real videos for real-world coverage analysis; (2) Controlled subtitle diversity, spanning 16 languages and four factors covering spatial layout, temporal behavior, visual style, and language mode; (3) Fine-grained evaluation, introducing an information-conditioned, spatially decoupled protocol that separates blind from mask-guided removal and measures Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, Temporal Fidelity, coverage, and failures. Experiments on six representative methods reveal substantial discrepancies between local restoration, outside-region preservation, temporal consistency, and full-set reliability that are obscured by conventional full-frame metrics. MFVSR therefore provides a more comprehensive and diagnostic foundation for evaluating and advancing video subtitle removal methods.

title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
summary: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.

title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://psetinek.github.io/multi-fidelity-neural-surrogates/ Code: https://github.com/psetinek/multi-fidelity-neural-surrogates
summary: Neural surrogates for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are usually trained on synthetic data from numerical simulators. As models grow and scaling laws demand larger datasets, the cost of data generation often outweighs the training cost and becomes the bottleneck in the scaling quest. Unlike data in other domains, however, each PDE sample has a tunable cost that depends on its numerical fidelity, with the resulting cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. We exploit this property by formalizing neural surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data generation compute budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum rather than a binary distinction. Building on this, we show that multi-fidelity training enables Pareto-optimal error scaling against data generation compute. By using simulations at lower fidelities as an additional training signal, training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches the accuracy of high-fidelity-only training, with up to $6.3\times$ less data generation compute across our settings. We validate these findings across six PDE problems spanning structured grids and unstructured meshes, two distinct error sources (discretization and iterative-solver error), and four surrogate architectures, totaling over 7,000 training runs.

title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
summary: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.

title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
comment: This is for a Neurips 2026 competition
summary: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

title: CodeLift: Your Test Suite Is Secretly a Dense SWE Curriculum
summary: The pass-all-test binary reward has become a standard recipe for training software engineering agents, but its sparsity eliminates difference of partially correct patches. The test pass-rate is a natural alternative. However, we find that it is not a reliable indicator of patch quality. A functionality being tested can be covered by either one challenging test or one hundred trivial tests, where the majority might be already satisfied pass-to-pass tests. We introduce CodeLift, a reinforcement learning method that dynamically calibrates pass-rate rewards, turning the test suite into an adaptive curriculum. At each iteration, CodeLift groups tests that kill the same patches and patches that pass the same tests, then gives more weight to test groups that fewer patch groups pass. This reduces the impact of majority simple tests and focuses more on what is still challenging. Within each rollout, CodeLift applies the same scoring rule to repository snapshots, assigning credit to useful actions even when later ones introduce regressions. Experiments on SWE benchmarks show that CodeLift consistently improves pass@1/2/4/8 over binary and pass-rate baselines. Analyses show that CodeLift provides dense, stable learning signals and unlocks the inherent curriculum in the test suite.

title: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance-Speech Consistency
journal_ref: Proc. Interspeech 2026, pp. 2424-2428 (2026)
summary: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.

title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
comment: 22 pages, including references and appendices. Code: https://github.com/jinlinll/lost-in-implicit-routing
summary: Reusable skills let LLM agents load task-specific instructions on demand, but they make execution depend on implicit routing over skill metadata. We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse: agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%, whereas explicit selection from the same library retains 73.9% recall. Loading other skills, including plausible alternatives to golden skills, is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores skill loading, yet with the metadata intact, explicitly asking agents to plan skill use still yields lower recall than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution. We also evaluate explicit preselection as a practical mitigation, including its coverage and latency trade-offs. Our analysis informs skill protocols and evaluation for agents with growing skill libraries.

title: MIRRA: Fast, High-Fidelity Molecular Generation with Chemistry-Informed Discrete Flow Matching
summary: Fast, high-fidelity molecular generation requires accurate chemical choices and efficient sampling. Chemical building blocks reduce graph size, but make each node a choice among tens of thousands of related identities. We introduce MIRRA (Molecular Identity Representation, Refresh and Assembly), a discrete flow-matching generator that learns from chemical knowledge and evaluates identity probabilities only when needed, while keeping every identity in its vocabulary available. Chemical features share information across related blocks, and learned identity corrections distinguish them in molecular context. By deciding which positions will refresh before computing their probabilities, the sampler avoids unused predictions while preserving each sampling transition. Against the strongest baselines in each task, MIRRA reduces chemical and graph distribution errors on ZINC250k by 29-31% and 53-60%, respectively, with generation up to 8.6 times faster. Property targeting yields an estimated 7.8-20.8 times more distinct novel hits per second. On a held-out polymer test set, MIRRA achieves 100% periodic validity with known chain topology, versus 57.0% for a polymer variational autoencoder. These results demonstrate fast, high-fidelity generation with the full chemical vocabulary available throughout sampling.

title: EgoOmniWorld: Unifying Egocentric Understanding via Ego-Action-World Interactions
summary: Egocentric video understanding spans diverse capabilities, modalities, and evaluation formats, yet these are often studied in isolation despite their tight coupling in real-world interaction. We propose the Ego-Action-World interaction loop as a unifying principle: the wearer perceives the world, forms goals, acts, changes the world, and uses feedback to guide subsequent behavior. Based on this view, we introduce EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark organized around four complementary interaction structures: Node captures ego, action, and world states; Edge captures directed relations among them; Chain captures linked dependencies; and Loop captures feedback-closed interactions. We develop an interaction-first, evidence-grounded data pipeline that extracts structured interactions from egocentric videos, grounds them in visual and auditory evidence, and generates questions according to their interaction structure. Required modalities and single- or multi-turn formats follow naturally from the supporting evidence and dependencies. EgoOmniWorld contains 24,166 QA groups, including 20,284 training and 3,882 test samples. Experiments on representative open- and closed-source multimodal large language models reveal substantial and uneven limitations across interaction structures. Models trained on EgoOmniWorld improve in-domain interaction understanding and generalize to existing egocentric benchmarks. EgoOmniWorld provides a unified foundation for evaluating and advancing egocentric video understanding. Data, code, and models will be released.

title: Input-Conditioned Search for Efficient Test-Time Scaling of Recursive Reasoners
summary: People often tackle difficult problems by thinking more deeply or exploring more possibilities. Similarly, recursive reasoners, which reason by repeatedly applying a learned update rule to latent states, can also scale inference through more updates (depth) or additional trajectories generated by perturbing latent states (width). When people hit a dead end in their thinking, they may step back and approach the problem from a fresh angle. However, neither depth scaling nor perturbation-based width scaling of recursive reasoners can reliably achieve this: both may converge to incorrect attractors. To address this, we propose to explore diverse reasoning traces by applying different update maps to the same latent state, without any additional training. We realize this idea through \emph{Input-Conditioned Search (ICS)}, which searches over input conditions to induce alternative update maps from the pretrained reasoner. Across six reasoning tasks, ICS achieves the highest mean accuracy, while requiring up to two orders of magnitude fewer model FLOPs than the evaluated scaling baselines. Controlled experiments confirm that ICS can redirect trajectories from the same state. Our theoretical analysis and rigorous numerical verification also confirm that ICS can locally eliminate incorrect attracting fixed points. Together, these findings establish ICS as an effective axis for efficient test-time scaling and motivate further research on shaping recursive reasoning during training and at test time.

title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
summary: Generative discovery in science requires coupling high-level scientific reasoning with the ability to generate samples respecting the structure of a design space. Yet these capabilities remain largely separated: foundation LLMs encode broad chemical and biological knowledge, while domain-specific flow- and diffusion-based generators capture the priors needed to produce valid sequences and geometries. We study how to align such scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals without requiring an explicit proxy reward, which is often unavailable or poorly captured by learned predictors in experimental sciences. We introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), where a frozen LLM acts as an adaptive teacher for a domain-specific generator. Given a goal such as 'generate peptides with promising anticancer activity', the teacher constructs a curriculum of intermediate sub-goals aware of the flow's current capabilities, and progressively directs them toward the original discovery goal. At each round, the LLM judges sampled candidates under the current objective. These judgments induce preferences that are iteratively distilled into the generator through DPO. This procedure provides dense learning signals even when the initial model places negligible probability on designs satisfying the final goal, enabling adaptation toward poorly covered, out-of-distribution regions. Experiments on therapeutic peptides and small-molecule structure design demonstrate that LFD enables a new form of generative control: aligning arbitrary domain-specific scientific generators to scientific discovery tasks expressed via high-level natural-language goals.

title: Dual-Domain Sparse-View 4D CBCT Reconstruction with Spatial-Temporal Consistency Learning
summary: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D CBCT) provides phase-resolved volumetric images for image-guided radiotherapy. Yet good reconstruction quality usually needs many projections. This increases scan time and radiation dose. We propose STCNet, a sparse-view 4D CBCT reconstruction framework that uses spatial-temporal consistency learning. STCNet reconstructs high-quality images from only 16 projections in each respiratory phase. STCNet integrates physics-driven positional encoding to enforce geometric consistency in the projection domain and introduces temporal encoding in latent space to capture respiratory motion dynamics across phases to capture dynamic respiratory motion across phases. A dual-domain collaborative strategy jointly optimizes both projection and image domains, enhancing structural fidelity and temporal coherence. We tested STCNet on the TCIA-LUNG dataset and a CIRS thorax phantom dataset. STCNet performed better than conventional methods and recent deep learning baselines in image quality, artifact reduction, and structural preservation. On TCIA-LUNG, STCNet reached PSNR values of 33.311, 32.695, and 32.658 dB at phases 2, 5, and 8. The corresponding SSIM values were 0.845, 0.823, and 0.825. On CIRS, STCNet achieved PSNR values up to 36.497 dB and SSIM values up to 0.877. These results support STCNet as a promising framework for low-dose, phase-resolved 4D CBCT reconstruction in image-guided radiotherapy.

title: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection
summary:
Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets.
  We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.

title: Protocol Choices Matter More Than the Aggregation Algorithm: Federated Learning for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Care-Unit and Multi-Hospital Federations
summary: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared mortality model without pooling their records, but published comparisons of aggregation strategies rarely control the evaluation protocol. This study compared seven strategies (FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdagrad, FedAdam, FedYogi and FedCluster) on two federations built with one pipeline: 12 care units of a hospital in MIMIC-IV and 49 hospitals in eICU-CRD. Each strategy was tuned and selected on validation data by the same rule, and every comparison was repeated across 10 seeds with Friedman and Holm-corrected tests. SCAFFOLD ranked first in both federations (AUC-ROC 0.886 and 0.819) and in 17 of 18 variants, but its margin over the runner-up never exceeded 0.008, and a control sharing its local optimizer attributed most of its margin over FedAvg to drift correction. On the multi-hospital federation, federated training matched centralized training. In the care-unit federation, three protocol choices changed discrimination by more than the choice of strategy did: discharge-coded predictors (+0.038 in AUC-ROC), client-level SMOTE (up to -0.074), and evaluating the last instead of the best validation round (up to -0.084). Platt scaling on validation data repaired the risks distorted by imbalance corrections without loss of discrimination. Studies should therefore fix the protocol before ranking algorithms.

title: Meta-Video: Efficient Standardized Evaluation for Video Understanding
summary: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.

title: Configuring RAG Systems: What Breaks, Where Originates, and How to Fix
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for improving Large Language Model (LLM) by intertwining it with other components, such as a vector/graph database. Therefore, the resulting RAG systems are often highly configurable, under which a non-trivial amount of failures are related to the configurations. However, there remains a lack of systematic understanding regarding the configuration issues for RAG systems. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 654 real-world configuration issues collected from 10 diverse RAG systems. Drawing on this, we provide a complete categorization of the symptoms, root causes, relevant stages, and fix patterns of configuration issues for RAG systems, as well as several new observations. Our findings not only reveal the characteristics of configuration issues, but also strongly link them to the unique pipeline stages of RAG, e.g., we found that most symptoms can be observed at the early or late stage, while the stage of the root cause might not be at the same stage as where the symptom is identified. We also provide nine actionable insights to the practitioners on testing, localizing, and fixing the configuration issues for RAG systems.

title: Measuring Learned Equivariance: An Information Theoretic Approach
summary: Learning symmetries through data augmentation offers an alternative to architectural equivariance, but does not guarantee that a network respects those symmetries. Measuring learned equivariance is especially difficult for intermediate representations, whose group actions are not specified. In a finite discrete setting, we show that equivariance requires representations of original and transformed inputs to determine one another exactly, yielding a test based on normalized mutual information (NMI). For high-dimensional activations, we use centered kernel alignment (CKA) as a scalable test, with an exact guarantee for orthogonal feature transformations. Across architectures and tasks, augmentation usually increases transformation consistency, showing that learned equivariance can be probed directly from representations without recovering the hidden transformation rules that relate them.

title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

title: Order-Consistent Latent Geometry for Reliable Short-Horizon Planning in World Models
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at STEAI 2026 (ECCV 2026 Workshop)
summary: Latent planners often rank candidate action sequences by terminal Euclidean distance to a goal latent. Exact agreement with transition distance would make this score ideal, but is stronger than planning requires: along a transition-shortest rollout, the essential requirement is that latent distance does not reverse true transition progress. We show that this pathwise no-reversal requirement is precisely the classical self-approaching condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify self-approachingness as a planner-facing compatibility condition for terminal Euclidean latent planning and to connect its violation to an exact finite-horizon candidate-order reversal. Because visual world models predict discrete latent sequences, we analyze their polygonal interpolation. We prove that an acute bend creates a nonempty region in which terminal Euclidean distance ranks a transition-worse candidate ahead of one that makes genuine progress, even under exact rollouts. We further interpret latent dimension as angular capacity through a classical spherical-code bound. A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded three-dimensional baseline, validates the predicted ordering failure and separates angular arrangement from ambient dimensionality.

title: The Surprising Expressivity of a Single Neuron with Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought
summary: The success of autoregressive language models trained with Chain-of-Thought~(CoT) supervision raises a fundamental question: How simple can a next-token predictor be while still enabling the efficient simulation of general computation through its autoregressively generated CoT? Surprisingly, we show that a single neuron suffices. For a broad family of activations, including threshold and ReLU, a single autoregressive neuron can simulate any feedforward circuit with the same activation. Specifically, a size-$s$ circuit on $n$ inputs can be simulated by a neuron of dimension $O(ns+s^2)$ using $O(s^2)$ generation steps, with both bounds independent of circuit depth and tight under natural assumptions. For threshold activations, this improves upon the simulation of Joshi et al. (COLT 2025), whose bounds scale exponentially with circuit depth. Consequently, autoregressive threshold neurons can simulate polynomial-time Turing machines, while remaining efficiently learnable from CoT supervision. Our main expressivity result relies on a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics. As an experimental illustration, we efficiently train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to mimic a neural network teacher with nontrivial test accuracy on CIFAR-10.

title: Denoise X: Self-Supervised U-Net for Quantum Mottle Suppression in Chest Radiography
summary: Deep learning for medical image restoration is often constrained by the need for paired training data. Acquiring perfectly registered clean-noisy radiographs in vivo is impractical due to patient motion and radiation-dose limits. To address this, we employ a self-supervised Noise2Noise paradigm that trains on independently corrupted observations without paired clean images. We propose Denoise X, a lightweight self-supervised U-Net model (7.79M parameters) for suppressing quantum mottle and electronic readout noise in low-dose chest radiographs. It is trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset (112,120 images) using a stochastic Poisson-Gaussian noise simulator. Zero-shot evaluation on the unseen Montgomery County dataset achieved a PSNR of 36.09 dB and SSIM of 0.8806, outperforming the Bilateral filter while preserving high-frequency anatomical details.
